Let’s dive into Chapter 9: the value of curiosity and asking questions.
Think about curiosity as the engine behind every great adventure—whether we’re exploring outer space, or just trying to figure something out here on Earth.
For astronauts, being curious—being willing to admit when you don’t know something and actually seeking out that knowledge—isn’t optional. It’s absolutely crucial.
Imagine you’re in a training room, surrounded by experts. Maybe you feel tempted to just nod along, act like you’ve got it all covered, and hope nobody notices if you’re lost. But you know what? The most valuable crew members are the ones who speak up. They’re the ones who aren’t afraid to raise a hand and say, “Hey, I don’t get this. Can you walk me through it?”
Those simple questions—that moment of admitting uncertainty—can spark real breakthroughs. They help uncover things nobody else even realized were missing. They fill in the gaps and make the whole team smarter and stronger.
Let me tell you a quick story. Picture a systems check, and suddenly there’s this odd blip on a readout. Most people might just brush it off, expecting it’ll disappear on its own. But one crew member, curious enough to dig a little deeper, decides to investigate. Turns out, that tiny anomaly points to a minor fault—something that, if ignored, could’ve led to a much bigger problem down the road.
So, what’s the lesson here? Curiosity isn’t just about learning for fun—it can actually keep people safe.
A lot of us grow up thinking we need to have all the answers, that it’s risky to admit when we don’t know something. But in spaceflight? Not knowing is dangerous. The real strength is in asking questions, in being open about what you don’t understand.
Over time, it becomes clear that the best teams are the ones where curiosity is welcome, where every question matters, and learning never stops.
And here’s the thing—this isn’t just for astronauts. No matter what field you’re in, that willingness to ask, to dig deeper, and to keep your curiosity alive? It leads to better results. It keeps your mind open, your team sharp, and your work meaningful.
